title: Shopping cart
like: the cart on an online store like Amazon
brief: Shoppers browse products, drop things in a cart and come back later from another phone. Browsing is most of the traffic and can be a little old. The cart itself must always show what the shopper just added.

clarify.q: Can the product pages be a little old?
clarify.a: Yes, by a minute or two. A price that changes is fixed at checkout.
No. If someone adds a shirt and the page reloads without it, they leave.

clarify.q: How long does a cart live?
clarify.a: About 30 days. Most carts are never bought (approx.).

notes: About 510 cart changes a second at the evening peak (approx.).
A cart is a few KB (approx.).

numbers.label: Cart changes per second at peak
Product views per second at peak

hints: Product pages and the cart have different promises. Which one may be a minute old?
A cache can answer product views. A key-value store keeps each cart under its owner as the key, with no joins needed.
Load balancer, a few servers, a cache for products, a SQL database for the catalog, and a key-value store for carts.

editorial.summary: Most traffic only looks at products, so a cache answers it. Each cart is one small record looked up by its owner, which is exactly what a key-value store does well, so carts never wait on the catalog database.

designs.name: Cache for products, key-value store for carts
designs.why: The cache serves product pages from memory and may be a minute old. Carts live in a key-value store read and written by one key, so adding an item is visible at once and the store grows without effort.

tradeoffs: A longer cache time saves the catalog database but can show an old price. A minute is a good middle.
A key-value store scales carts easily, but you cannot ask it questions like "who has this item in a cart".
Keeping the cart only in the browser is cheap, but it vanishes when the shopper switches device.
Saving carts for 30 days costs a little storage and brings many shoppers back.
editorial.realWorld: Large shops see a few hundred cart changes a second on a normal evening and many times more on a sale day. Carts are usually kept in key-value stores for exactly this reason (approx.).
